content: Community support for individuals living with HIV is essential to improve retention in HIV care. Strong recommendations exist for implementing community-level interventions, although the evidence supporting these interventions varies in certainty. Specific interventions that have shown benefits include: 1. A package of community-based interventions, which provide adherence and psychosocial support within the community. These interventions are supported by low-certainty evidence for children and very low-certainty evidence for adults. 2. Adherence clubs, which involve peer support, distribution of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, and assessments by non-clinical or lay healthcare providers. These are supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 3. Additional care for high-risk individuals, supported by very low-certainty evidence. Task sharing in the initiation and maintenance of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is also recommended. Trained and supervised community health workers can dispense ART between regular clinical visits, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Similarly, trained and supervised lay healthcare providers can distribute ART, supported by low-certainty evidence. Patient monitoring systems must be adapted to provide accurate and timely data on differentiated service delivery (DSD) models. This includes updates to tools such as the HIV treatment and care patient card, ART register, and cohort reports to monitor patients engaged in DSD models. Data from community ART sites, such as community ART groups and distribution points, should be promptly entered into facility-based patient monitoring systems to ensure data linkage and flow. This prevents parallel reporting systems and improves patient management and care. Routine review of data from all community ART delivery models at the facility level is critical to improve services and data quality. Data sharing between public and private DSD delivery points, including real-time tracking of missed appointments, is essential. Facility-based patient monitoring systems should be adapted to identify and respond to missed appointments, ensuring efficient data and patient flow. Unique identifiers (UIDs) for clients initiating ART in community settings should ideally be issued by health facilities, which retain responsibility for confidentiality and security. Interoperability between systems, including electronic medical records (EMR), community health information, logistics, and laboratory systems, is necessary to harmonize appointment dates, track missed medication pickups, and minimize disruptions in drug supply. Monitoring the implementation of DSD models requires a range of indicators, including patient and healthcare worker satisfaction, facility uptake of DSD, service delivery costs, and clinical outcomes. WHO provides guidance on monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of these aspects, including key indicators to track the coverage, uptake, and clinical outcomes of DSD models. Retention in DSD ART models is a critical indicator, measured as the percentage of individuals retained in care at specific time points (e.g., 12, 24, or 36 months). Viral suppression among individuals engaged in DSD ART models is another key indicator, assessed through routine viral load (VL) testing. Tracing interventions are recommended to identify individuals who have disengaged from care and support their re-engagement. This includes tracking missed appointments, ART pickups, and clinical visits. Suggested criteria for triggering tracing interventions include missed appointments by more than seven days, lack of ARV drugs for over seven days, or high VL test results. Tracing methods may include telephone calls and home visits, with outcomes recorded to monitor the effectiveness of these interventions. Integration of services, such as TB-HIV and maternal and child health, is necessary to streamline care. Appointments should be scheduled to coincide when multiple services are accessed at different delivery points. Periodic assessments of clinical outcomes for individuals enrolled in DSD ART models are recommended to evaluate the impact of these models. Adapted ART cohort reports can be used to calculate retention and VL suppression outcomes. It is important to ensure that individuals in DSD models are included in ART cohort monitoring and that measures are in place to prevent double counting or undercounting. For individuals re-engaging in care after treatment interruption, it is important to assess factors such as CD4 cell count, high VL, adherence challenges, and opportunistic infections. These individuals may require more clinical follow-up and may not be eligible for DSD ART models. Differentiating between new ARV-naive individuals and those re-engaging in care is also critical for assessing DSD eligibility.
